$description: The neutral brand at its defaults: the light colour scheme, standard contrast.

scheme.$description: What each colour scheme paints with; private. The dark scheme redefines it.

order.$description: The two ends of an order's steps: in the light scheme, a mid grey whose dark text still holds 5 to 1, and the pale grey of a rule, which stands 1.4 to 1 off the page.

background.$description: The ground of a page: white, so text and marks reach their strongest contrast on it, and a slide reads in a lit room.

surface.$description: A quiet ground a step above the page, for a part that holds others, such as a card or a code block: its edge, not its shade, sets it apart, so it survives a projector that washes pale greys out.

text-primary.$description: The text a reader reads first: a near-black, not black, at more than 15 to 1 on the page, so long text reads without glare (WCAG 2, 1.4.6).

text-secondary.$description: Text that steps back, such as a lead, a caption or a comment: a mid grey that still holds 4.5 to 1 on the page and on the surface, so stepping back never costs legibility (WCAG 2, 1.4.3).

accent.$description: The one hue the brand marks with by itself, a deep blue: blue is the hue most readers take as calm and trustworthy, and at this depth it holds 4.5 to 1 as text.

line.$description: The edge of a part and a rule between rows: a pale grey, faint by design, since a line that only groups should never vie with the text it groups.

family.$description: The members of the foundations' colour families: the neutral family paints with the surface, the line and the primary text, and each hue with what the colour scheme gives it. Beside them lie an order's roles, which form no family.

order.$description: An order's two ends and the text on every step between them: greys, so the steps vary in lightness alone, which the eye reads as an order, and in no hue, which it would read as kinds (Jacques Bertin, the visual variables; Cynthia Brewer, a sequential scheme). The first end lies furthest from the page, so the order's source stands out most, and the last stays far enough from it that a level's shape shows without an edge. The text is the primary text, darker than both ends in light and lighter than both in dark, and at least 5 to 1 on each, so every step between keeps it legible and high contrast strengthens it with the rest of the text.

space.$description: Four steps that double, 4, 8, 16 and 32 px: few enough that every gap is one of them, so space inside a group stays visibly smaller than space between groups (Robin Williams, proximity; Josef Müller-Brockmann, a module that every distance repeats).

size.$description: The widths a piece is laid out in: a figure, a slide, a site's page and a line of text, which stays under about 75 characters of the body.

figure.$description: The width of a figure's page.

site.$description: The width of a site's page, on a desktop.

line.$description: The length of a line of text, at most.

stroke.$description: Two widths of line: a thin one for an edge, which only groups, and a thick one for a line drawn on its own, such as a connector, which a reader follows.

thick.$description: A line drawn on its own, such as a connector, whose arrowheads it sizes.

font.$description: Source Sans Pro, an open humanist sans: plain and even, legible at small sizes and from across a room, with a semibold weight for heads.

typeface.$description: The families the brand's types take beside the shared ones; private.

code.$description: A monospace family, for the type of code.

type.$description: The types at a desktop: a body of 16 px, a head that differs from it by size and weight, a strong run the body's size in the semibold, and code a step under the body, since a monospace face sets wider. Few sizes, each clearly apart (Robert Bringhurst, a scale).

strong.$description: A strong phrase in the body's text: the body's size and line height, in the heading's semibold family.

code.$description: Code, as a terminal or a file shows it: Source Code Pro, a monospace family, a little smaller than the body's text.

component.$description: The tokens of the components of the libraries the brand names: at a desktop, the deck's title and lead take the shared types it drew them in before.
